# Fit for Service {-}

> "You therefore must endure hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier."
>
> — 2 Timothy 2:3-4

Before the final step, one short chapter. It has no number, because it isn't part of the method. It is about what you are being set free for.

## Out of the fight {-}

Start with a way of looking at the whole habit that this book has kept back until now.

Suppose you had an enemy who wanted you harmless. He wouldn't need to ruin you. Ruin is noisy, and ruined men sometimes wake up. It would be enough to keep you occupied with something small and private. It would cost you your nerve, your evenings and your self-respect, and you would never mention it to anyone. There's a saying you'll hear in a lot of churches: the devil doesn't need to destroy you if he can distract you.

Scripture has the case study. "At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel ... But David stayed at Jerusalem. At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king's house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at." This was the man who killed Goliath. No Philistine ever beat him in the field. He was beaten on a rooftop on an idle evening, at the time when kings go out, because he hadn't gone. It took no sword, only a glimpse of skin. One commentator needs a single sentence for it: "He should have been out at the battle, but he wasn't."

A pastor preaching on that passage says what the enemy is after: "He wants to distract you, disengage you, discourage you, take you out of the war". Another writer gives temptation's whole method in a line: "Temptation will please you to abuse you, seduce you to undo you, distract you to destroy you." And Peter wrote to people he loved: "Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour."

Look at it from the enemy's side. Here is a man with a wife to love, children to raise and work to do. Perhaps he has something to build that would do some good in the world. How do you stop him? You don't have to fight him at all. Show him a little skin on a screen and he takes himself off the field. Twenty minutes later he is spent, ashamed and no use to anybody until tomorrow, and tomorrow you can do it again. It's the cheapest victory there is.

If you don't believe in a devil, you don't need horns and a pitchfork for this. Ask who gains. There are companies that earn more the longer you stay aroused, alone and tired. Something does better when men are soft, numb and spent. Call it the devil, call it evil, call it a business model. It is working on you either way, and nobody had to fight you.

Two cautions, so that this isn't misread. First, none of it is an excuse. James won't let a man say the devil made him do it: "each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed." The enemy can dangle the bait, but the appetite is yours. That is good news, because it means the way out is yours as well. Second, don't go hunting demons under the bed. C.S. Lewis warned of "two equal and opposite errors" about devils. One is to disbelieve in them, and the other is to take an unhealthy interest in them. Take the enemy seriously, and then get on with your life.

And think what all this says about you. Nobody bothers to distract a man who doesn't matter. You were worth taking out of the fight. When Nehemiah was rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, his enemies kept inviting him down for a talk. He sent back the answer you'll soon be able to give: "I am doing a great work, so that I can't come down."

## Drunk on duty {-}

Stay in that story a little longer, because there is a second soldier in it.

David learned that the woman was pregnant. So he sent to the front for her husband, Uriah, hoping he would go home to his wife and cover the thing up. Uriah wouldn't. "The ark, Israel, and Judah, are staying in tents; and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open field. Shall I then go into my house to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing!" So David tried again: "he ate and drank before him; and he made him drunk." Even drunk, Uriah slept among the servants and would not go down to his house.

Look at the two men. One is Uriah the Hittite, a foreigner in Israel's army, who won't take even an honest comfort while his friends are in the field. The other is the king, the giant-killer, at home and off duty. He is so far gone that he is pouring drink into a good soldier to hide what he did. The man who should have been leading the army is making its soldiers unfit.

Now let me say this to you as plainly as I can.

You may be a Christian. You may be on God's side, and he does love you. Nothing in this chapter puts that in question. "There is therefore now no condemnation" was true in the Introduction, and it is true on this page.

And you were made on purpose. "You knit me together in my mother's womb", David wrote. Paul says the work was planned as well as the man: "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them." There is something with your name on it that nobody else is placed to do.

But a man ruled by lust is a soldier who turns up drunk for duty. He is loved, he is enlisted, and he is unfit for service. He can't fight at full strength. He can't be relied on at the hour he is needed. And he is a danger to the men beside him, who are counting on fire support that isn't coming. Paul names the two things in one breath: "since we belong to the day, let's be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet, the hope of salvation." Sober comes first, and then the armour.

Don't tell yourself it's private. When Israel lost the fight at Ai, thirty-six men died because one man had buried something under the floor of his tent. A pastor preaching on that chapter drew the conclusion: "You've never committed a private sin because there is no such thing." Your wife is short a husband. Your children are short a father. Your church is short a man, and so is whatever work you were made for. They have been covering your position for years without knowing why the line was thin.

So get the order right. The people who know most about getting sober learned this the hard way. One of their earliest handbooks says it flatly: "Sobriety is the most important thing in your life, without exception." And they have a saying in their meetings, that whatever you put ahead of your sobriety, you will lose. Here is how it applies to you. **If you aren't putting your recovery first, you are putting everything else last: your family, your God, your purpose.**

Now the good news, which is the reason this book exists. This enemy is not hard to beat. Nobody is sending you on a ten-year campaign. You've read twenty-six chapters and you know what the thing is: a trick, an itch that feeds itself, a lie about comfort. It doesn't take courage to put down a thing you have seen through.

And being fit is not the price of being loved. It is what a loved man is for. Paul says it is grace itself that does the training, "instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly". He also names what you become: "a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master's use, prepared for every good work."

If you're not a believer, keep the picture and change the flag. You still have people who depend on you and work that is yours to do, and you have been turning up to both half-present. The order of things is the same for you.

So here is what I'm asking. "Lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees". Stand up. Sober up. Report for duty. When Isaiah heard the question, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?", he had just been forgiven, and he made no speech about his record. He said, "Here I am. Send me!"

The next chapter is where you say it.
